config.title: RBAC Permission Hook

intro.title: RBAC Permission Hook
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom React hook called `useRBAC` that checks user permissions based on Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). You will learn how to encapsulate permission logic into a reusable function using React's `useState` and `useEffect` hooks. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript, and TSX files for type-safe component development. By the end, you'll be able to conditionally render UI elements or restrict actions depending on a user's assigned roles and permissions.
intro.usecase: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) permission hooks are essential in enterprise applications where different users need different levels of access. For example, in an admin dashboard, a manager might see buttons to delete users or edit financial reports, while a regular employee only sees view-only panels. This pattern controls UI elements like action buttons, navigation menus, and data filters based on user roles, ensuring security and a tailored interface. Developers implement these hooks to conditionally render components, preventing unauthorized actions without cluttering code with repetitive permission checks.

objectives: Implement a custom React hook that manages role-based access control state
Configure TypeScript interfaces to define user roles and permissions
Construct a permission-checking function that validates user access
Integrate the RBAC hook into a React component to control UI visibility
Initialize and update permission state based on user role changes
Apply conditional rendering logic to display or hide components based on permissions
Manipulate permission data structures to add or remove user capabilities

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, enabling the use of React and useState in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported React, but remember to also import useState from 'react' to manage state in your component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Ensure you import both React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Define the UserRole type
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript type named 'UserRole' that can be one of three string literal values: 'admin', 'editor', or 'viewer'.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by the type name and the union operator '|' to specify the allowed string values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: defining a type with specific string values
type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' | 'pending';
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Define the UserRole type here
steps.expectedOutcome: A UserRole type is defined with the three allowed role values.
successCriteria: The UserRole type is defined with the union of 'admin', 'editor', and 'viewer' string literals.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your type includes all three roles: 'admin', 'editor', and 'viewer'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the expected UserRole type definition. Try using the 'type' keyword with a union of string literals.

steps.title: Define the Permission type
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript type named Permission with the literal values 'create', 'read', 'update', and 'delete'.
steps.hint: Use the type keyword with a union of string literals separated by the pipe (|) symbol.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a type for traffic light colors
type TrafficLight = 'red' | 'yellow' | 'green';
steps.expectedOutcome: A Permission type is defined with the four permission values.
successCriteria: The Permission type is defined as a union type containing 'create', 'read', 'update', and 'delete'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a Permission type, but it's missing some required values. Make sure it includes 'create', 'read', 'update', and 'delete'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Permission type isn't defined correctly. Define a type named Permission with the values 'create', 'read', 'update', and 'delete'.

steps.title: Create the rolePermissions mapping
steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'rolePermissions' that maps each UserRole to an array of Permission values. Use TypeScript to define it as a Record<UserRole, Permission[]>.
steps.hint: Define a constant with the Record type where keys are UserRole and values are arrays of Permission.
steps.expectedOutcome: A rolePermissions constant is defined with proper TypeScript typing that maps each UserRole to its corresponding Permission array.
successCriteria: rolePermissions is defined as a Record<UserRole, Permission[]> with at least admin, editor, and viewer roles mapped to appropriate permission arrays.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure rolePermissions uses the Record<UserRole, Permission[]> type and includes all three roles.
steps.feedbackWrong: The rolePermissions mapping isn't quite right. It should be a Record<UserRole, Permission[]> type with admin, editor, and viewer roles mapped to arrays of Permission values.

steps.title: Define the useRBAC hook interface
steps.instruction: Define an interface named 'UseRBACReturn' that describes what the useRBAC hook will return. It should have two properties: 'hasPermission' (a function that takes a Permission and returns boolean) and 'currentRole' (of type UserRole).
steps.hint: Create an interface with the specified properties. Remember to use proper TypeScript syntax for function types.
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named UseRBACReturn is defined with hasPermission and currentRole properties.
successCriteria: The interface UseRBACReturn is defined with hasPermission: (permission: Permission) => boolean and currentRole: UserRole properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that both properties are correctly typed. The hasPermission should be a function that takes Permission and returns boolean, and currentRole should be UserRole.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to create an interface named UseRBACReturn with the two specified properties.

steps.title: Implement the useRBAC hook function
steps.instruction: Create the useRBAC function that accepts a UserRole parameter and returns the UseRBACReturn interface.
steps.hint: Define a function named useRBAC that takes a role parameter of type UserRole and returns an object matching the UseRBACReturn interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useRBAC function is defined with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria: A function named useRBAC exists, accepts a UserRole parameter, and returns an object matching UseRBACReturn.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the function accepts a UserRole parameter and returns an object matching the UseRBACReturn interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or has incorrect parameters or return type. Review the UseRBACReturn interface and ensure the function signature matches.

steps.title: Add state for current role in the hook
steps.instruction: Inside your useRBAC hook function, initialize a state variable called 'currentRole' using useState, with the initial value set to the 'role' parameter passed to the hook.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The state variable should hold the UserRole type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: useState with a parameter
const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount);
steps.expectedOutcome: The useRBAC hook will have a currentRole state variable initialized with the role parameter.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with the role parameter, and the state variable is named currentRole.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState with the role parameter and naming the variable currentRole.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the useRBAC function, use useState to create a state variable called currentRole initialized with the role parameter.

steps.title: Implement the hasPermission function
steps.instruction: Inside the useRBAC hook, implement the hasPermission function to check if the current role has the given permission using the rolePermissions mapping.
steps.hint: The function should take a permission parameter and return true if that permission exists in the current role's permission array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The hasPermission function will correctly return true or false based on whether the current role has the specified permission.
successCriteria: The hasPermission function is implemented and uses the rolePermissions mapping to check permissions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started implementing hasPermission, but it needs to use the rolePermissions mapping to check against the current role.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hasPermission function isn't implemented correctly. It should check if the permission exists in the current role's permission array.

steps.title: Return the hook values
steps.instruction: Inside the useRBAC hook, return an object containing the hasPermission function and the currentRole state value.
steps.hint: The hook should return an object with two properties: hasPermission and currentRole. Use the state variable and the function you've implemented.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useRBAC hook returns an object with hasPermission and currentRole properties, making them available to components that use this hook.
successCriteria: The hook returns an object containing both hasPermission and currentRole values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning an object with both hasPermission and currentRole properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook should return an object with hasPermission and currentRole. Check that you're returning the correct values from your state and function implementations.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named RBACDemo that will serve as the main component to demonstrate the useRBAC hook.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns JSX. You can start with a simple div or fragment.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named RBACDemo is created, ready to use the useRBAC hook in the next steps.
successCriteria: The RBACDemo component is defined as a function that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the component, but make sure it's a functional component named RBACDemo that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Create a functional component named RBACDemo that returns JSX.

steps.title: Use the hook in the component
steps.instruction: Inside the RBACDemo component, call the useRBAC hook with the 'editor' role and destructure the hasPermission and setRole values from the returned object.
steps.hint: Call useRBAC('editor') and destructure the returned object to get hasPermission and setRole.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: calling a custom hook and destructuring
const { value, setValue } = useCustomHook('initial');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has access to the hasPermission function and setRole function from the useRBAC hook, initialized with the 'editor' role.
successCriteria: The useRBAC hook is called with 'editor' and the returned hasPermission and setRole are destructured.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useRBAC with 'editor' and destructuring both hasPermission and setRole from the returned object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook isn't being used correctly. Remember to call useRBAC('editor') and destructure the returned object to get hasPermission and setRole.

steps.title: Render permission checks in JSX
steps.instruction: Inside your RBACDemo component's return statement, render the current role and permission check results. Display the current role value and call hasPermission for each permission type ('create', 'read', 'update', 'delete') to show true/false results.
steps.hint: You can display the current role value and map through an array of permissions to show each check result. Use the hasPermission function from your hook.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will display the current role and true/false results for each permission check when rendered.
successCriteria: The RBACDemo component returns JSX that displays the current role value and calls hasPermission for each permission type to show the results.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some JSX, but make sure you're displaying the current role value and checking all four permission types with hasPermission.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't display the current role or permission check results. Check that you're returning JSX with the role value and hasPermission calls.
